Anxious Depression and the Stiff-person Plus Syndrome
Jadranka Cˇulav-Sumic´, M D , M Sc , Ivan Bos ˘njak , M D , M Sc , Zvonimir Pas ˘tar , M D ,
and Vlado Jukic ´, M D , PhD
Objective: To present the case of a patient with anxiety and
depressive symptoms who developed the clinical picture of stiﬀ-
person plus syndrome (SPS-plus).
Background: Before the onset of typical SPS symptoms,
psychiatric symptoms (like depression and anxiety) may be
prominent and as such misleading, resulting in the diagnosis of a
psychiatric condition.
Method: We describe the case of a woman who initially
presented with anxious depression and remained resistant to
treatment with diﬀerent classes of antidepressants and addi-
tional therapy with lithium and atypical antipsychotics.
Results: Evidence of neurologic dysfunction and signiﬁcantly
increased levels of serum autoantibodies for glutamic acid
decarboxylase supported the diagnosis of SPS. The patient
appeared to beneﬁt from short-term immunosuppressive ther-
apy with methylprednisolone.
Conclusions: The authors believe that anxious depression and
SPS-plus seen in this patient are the result of the same
underlying autoimmune process, together forming a unique
syndrome. Anxious and depressive symptoms in SPS can be
explained by alterations in GABAergic neurotransmission.
Key Words: anxious depression, stiﬀ-person syndrome, glutamic
acid decarboxylase autoantibodies
(Cog Behav Neurol 2008;21:242–245)
S
tiﬀ-person syndrome (SPS; also known as stiﬀ-man
syndrome or Moersch-Woltman syndrome according
to the authors who ﬁrst described it at the Mayo Clinic in
1956) is a rare, relatively unknown neurologic disorder
that is sometimes diﬃcult to identify in its early stage.
1,2
SPS often begins insidiously, during the middle decades of
life and aﬀects both men and women.
3,4 The typical
clinical form is characterized by the rigidity of paraspinal
muscles with exaggerated lumbar lordosis, muscular
spasms caused by internal (eg, emotional distress) or
external (eg, noises, movements) stimuli, with otherwise
normal ﬁndings in motor and sensory examinations and
by a continuous motor-unit activity detected by electro-
myography.
5 Nevertheless, some patients may also show
signs of cerebellar ataxia or encephalitis, referred to as
‘‘stiﬀ-person plus syndrome’’ (SPS-plus).
6 The etiology is
thought to be autoimmune in nature due to the fact that
autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) are found in 80% of patients with SPS. 7–13
GAD is the rate-limiting enzyme for the synthesis of
g-aminobutyric acid (GABA), which is the brain’s main
inhibitory neurotransmitter. GABA is expressed selec-
tively in GABAergic neurons and some endocrine tissues.
An excess of GAD autoantibodies, also seen in other
autoimmune diseases (eg, insulin-dependent diabetes
mellitus, thyroiditis), is very striking in SPS and helps in
attaining the correct diagnosis.
14
At the onset of SPS, especially if associated with a
signiﬁcant emotional or psychosocial stressor, psychiatric
symptoms (eg, depression, anxiety, and phobias) may be
prominent and misleading so that a psychiatric condition
is diagnosed.
4,15–17
CASE REPORT
A 55-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for
the ﬁrst time in 2005 because of a suicide attempt. She was
already diagnosed as having depression 4 years earlier. Her
symptoms began in 2001, after a gynecologic operation
(hysterectomy and oophorectomy because of leiomyoma). At

that time she was depressed, complaining of abdominal pain and
attempted suicide for the ﬁrst time, with medications. Two
consequent operations did not reveal an organic cause for the
pain and so the patient started psychiatric treatment. Her
mental status partially improved with paroxetine and she was
able to work again with occasional sick leaves.
In the meantime she was hospitalized in another
psychiatric department where computed tomography of the
brain was performed, showing moderate cortical cerebral
atrophy. Her level of functioning remained poor and so she
was retired.
At the time of admission to our hospital, in 2005, her
personal medical history included hypercholesterolemia, hyper-
tension, and the previously mentioned operations. Her family
history was negative for psychiatric and autoimmune disorders.
Her father died at a young adult age, after the operation of a
brain tumor. The patient did not use alcohol or other
psychoactive substances but she smoked a few cigarettes a day.
The patient presented with a subjective sensation of
tremulousness (what she called an ‘‘inner tremor’’), fatigue,
avolition, initial insomnia, early morning awakening, loss of
interest, and low mood. There were no signs of psychosis. We
noticed aﬀective incongruence between her subjective feeling of

a depressed mood and nondepressive facial expressions. She was
well oriented and knew some recent political events. Ideas of
hopelessness and guilt were present. Because she persistently
complained of an ‘‘inner tremor,’’ a neurologic examination was
performed but no parkinsonian signs were found. The clinical
impression was that depression and incipient psychoorganic
syndrome, detected by psychologic examination, were the main
reason for the patient’s disability.
When the patient was hospitalized again in January 2007,
the neurologic signs became apparent: cerebellar ataxia
with inability to stand or walk alone, stiﬀ gait, tension of
paravertebral musculature with hyperlordosis, resting tremor of
the left arm (greater amplitude that is typical for parkinsonian
tremor), discrete resting tremor of the right arm, and diﬀusely
low muscle tonus and muscle strength. Her facial expression was
reduced and speech was normal but monotonous. Deep tendon
reﬂexes were present, with normal plantar response. Deﬁcits in
sensibility were not found.
The subjective sensation of tremulousness was still
present. She seemed anxious and depressed and felt relatively
good only while lying on bed, staring at 1 point. Transitory
horizontal nystagmus and dilated pupils were occasionally
observed and tachycardia (up to 130/min) with tachypnea was
present. She was conscious and well oriented to time, place, and
persons, during the whole time. Her answers to typical questions
were correct, although given after a period of latency. However,
intellectual decline was obvious.
Routine laboratory ﬁndings were normal and repeatedly
checked. Creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase enzymes
were normal. Thyroid hormones, thyrotropin, corticotropin,
and cortisol were also within the reference range. Gastroscopy
revealed erosive gastritis. Gynecologic examination, transab-
dominal ultrasound, and standard chest and abdominal x-rays
did not show abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the
brain showed somewhat larger third and lateral ventricles with
larger frontotemporal bilateral subarachnoid spaces. Analysis
of cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) showed: a clear and colorless
appearance of CSF, normal total cell count, normal total
protein, glucose, and chloride levels; Pandy reaction was weak
opalescent. CSF protein electrophoresis showed: increased
prealbumin (7.8%; reference range: 4 to 7) and g globulin
(19.5%; reference range: 7 to 12), whereas albumin, a 1 globulin,
a 2 globulin, b 1 globulin, and b 2 globulin were within the
reference range. g globulins were divided into fractions.
Examination of the blood-brain barrier showed the presence
of oligoclonal immunoglobulin G bands suggestive of intrathe-
cal synthesis of g globulins. A test for serum autoantibodies to
GAD was positive (680 IU/mL; normally <10 IU/mL; cut-oﬀ
value for very high elevation: >250 IU/mL). Serologic tests for
borreliosis and neurotrophic viruses were performed. Only tests
for herpes simplex virus 1-IgM and IgG were positive.
RESULTS
At ﬁrst, the patient’s aﬀective symptoms partially
improved with paroxetine. However, during time, despite
continuous antidepressant treatment, the symptoms of
anxious depression worsened and remained resistant to
various antidepressants (serotonin and serotonin-nora-
drenalin reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants,
moclobemide). Lithium worsened the ‘‘inner tremor.’’
The addition of atypical antipsychotics was also ineﬀec-

tive. Finally, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) was
considered but due to the presence of psychoorganic
symptoms ECT was eliminated as an option.
Speciﬁc treatment began as soon as the accurate
diagnosis of SPS was attained. Administration of
diazepam in doses up to 40 mg/d did not improve the
neurologic status substantially and essential sedation
occurred. Persistent disability despite ﬁrst-line therapy
with diazepam indicated the application of corticosteroids
(oral methylprednisolone 64 mg/d). According to the
clinical global impression the patient seemed to beneﬁt
from short-term immunosuppression. Cerebral ataxia and
resting tremor, along with anxiety, depressed mood, and
suicidal ideation were partially improved and the patient
was released from the hospital in a slightly better
condition.
DISCUSSION
Clinical appearance of neurologic dysfunction and
the ﬁnding of signiﬁcantly increased levels of anti-GAD
autoantibodies provided support for the diagnosis of SPS.
Some authors categorize SPS into 3 subtypes: stiﬀ trunk
syndrome, stiﬀ limb syndrome, and progressive encepha-
lomyelitis with rigidity.
18 In the third subtype (also called
the SPS-plus) additional neurologic signs, such as eye
movement disturbances or ataxia, are present. We
concluded that our patient belongs to the SPS-plus group
because of the presence of cerebellar ataxia, atypical
parkinsonian signs, and transient horizontal nystagmus.
The possibility of a paraneoplastic SPS
19–21 was
excluded because screenings and performed examinations
showed no evidence of a malignant process. Further
more, in paraneoplastic SPS serology tests for anti-GAD
antibodies are usually negative. Progressive supranuclear
palsy and multiple system atrophy were excluded because
of the absence of eye movement abnormalities and
orthostatic hypotension. Because of the long duration
of the disorder with no evidence of trismus and electrolyte
imbalance, there were no signs of tetanus and tetany
resulting from electrolyte abnormalities. A lumbar
puncture was performed twice in the interval of a week,
approximately 40 mL of CSF (the so-called intermittent
high volume tap) was taken, this did not relieve the
patient’s symptoms, therefore the diagnosis of normal-
pressure hydrocephalus was also excluded.
22,23
The patient’s syndrome started insidiously with
aﬀective changes and abdominal pain, perhaps the
underlying abdominal pain was a trigger for the onset
of SPS. In general, the anxiety and depression observed in
our patient may be the result of, or a reaction to, the
underlying neurologic disorder or the 2 conditions may
exist comorbidly. Because psychiatric symptoms occurred
before the onset of obvious motor symptoms, the authors
believe that anxious depression, cognitive decline, and
neurologic signs seen in the patient are the primary
manifestations of the disease itself, forming a unique
syndrome. Our hypothesis is consistent with previous
observations that depression or other psychopathologic
symptoms may precede SPS symptoms.
15 The therapeutic

resistance of depression to diﬀerent antidepressants also
supports this hypothesis. Even tricyclic antidepressants,
known to worsen the course of SPS, 24 applied according
to treatment guidelines for depression, before the onset of
the physical symptoms of SPS were ineﬀective. Anxious
and depressive symptoms in SPS could be explained by
alterations in GABAergic neurotransmission. Increasing
evidence from literature indicates that major depressive
disorder is associated with deﬁcits in GABAergic func-
tion. Plasma and CSF GABA concentrations were found
decreased in depressed patients.
25 Recent studies using
magnetic resonance spectroscopy methods revealed re-
duced GABA levels in diﬀerent brain regions in drug-free
depressed adults compared with controls. 26,27 Further-
more, Sanacora et al 28 demonstrated that reductions of
GABA were more prominent in more severely depressed
individuals. The potential role of GABAergic dysfunction
in depression could be partially explained through
GABAergic modulation of serotonergic, noradrenergic,
and dopaminergic systems.
25 Another line of evidence
comes from the positive results achieved when treating
depression with ECT and drugs enhancing GABAergic
transmission.
29,30 GABA is believed to be involved in the
pathophysiology of anxiety disorders as well. Studies on
animals demonstrated the connection between anxietylike
behaviors and GABA deﬁcits.
31 Clinical studies of plasma
and CSF GABA concentrations in patients with panic
disorder yielded conﬂicting results, but magnetic reso-
nance spectroscopy studies have shown decreased cortical
GABA levels in unmedicated patients with panic dis-
order.
32,33 A prominent decrease in cortical GABA levels
was found in patients with SPS, with diﬀerent degrees of
aﬀection in diﬀerent brain regions. 34 According to these
ﬁndings, the symptoms of anxiety and depression
observed in our patient with SPS-plus could be the result
of reduced or impaired GABAergic inhibition. The
pathogenic role of anti-GAD autoantibodies in SPS is
still unclear. It has been proposed that another autoanti-
gen, diﬀerent from GAD, but associated with the
GABAergic system may be the target of the autoimmune
process and the basis for the structural changes in the
brain.
35,36
Patients with SPS and positive anti-GAD auto-
antibodies were found to have additional autoimmune
disorders, most commonly type 1 diabetes mellitus.
4,14,37
However, repeatedly controlled fasting blood glucose
levels did not show abnormalities in glucose metabolism
in our patient. She had no other autoimmune disorders
and her family history, to our knowledge, was negative
for diabetes mellitus and other autoimmune diseases.
If untreated, SPS can result in great disability.
38 The
subgroup of patients with SPS-plus can be considered as
having the most severe form of SPS with a poor treatment
outcome. However, treatment with intravenous immuno-
globulin (IVIg), alone or in combination with immuno-
suppression, was useful in certain cases of SPS-plus.
39
In Croatia, like in most European countries, 40 IVIg has
not been licensed for the treatment of SPS and other
autoimmune disorders (except immunothrombocytopenia
refractory to corticosteroids) but it can be given in this
case as the next treatment option, at the discretion of
the treating neurologist. According to literature, plasma
exchange and chemotherapy agents have also been
beneﬁcial for some patients with SPS.
41,42

None.
